boston-roxbury-grant-lawsuit-2026.excerpt: The city says the U.S. Department of Transportation unlawfully withdrew a 2022 award for safety, transit and accessibility work on three major corridors.
boston-roxbury-grant-lawsuit-2026.text: boston sues over $20m grant for roxbury street upgrades the city says the u.s. department of transportation unlawfully withdrew a 2022 award for safety, transit and accessibility work on three major corridors. the city of boston has gone to federal court to recover a $20 million transportation grant that officials say was withdrawn after the project included a small electric-vehicle charging component. the lawsuit, filed sept. 28 in the u.s. district court for the district of massachusetts, asks the court to reverse the u.s. department of transportation's cancellation of the 2022 award for the roxbury resilient corridors project. the filing and case number, city of boston v. duffy, are listed in the public docket record (https://dockets.justia.com/docket/massachusetts/madce/1:2026cv14419/306825). the dispute centers on three roxbury streets: melnea cass boulevard, malcolm x boulevard and warren street. boston's project page says the grant was intended to support street repairs, safer crossings, transit improvements, accessibility work, traffic-flow changes, trees, lighting, public spaces and stormwater features. the city describes the corridors as central roadways in a historically disinvested neighborhood and says the project was being developed with local residents and community organizations (https://www.boston.gov/departments/transportation/project/roxbury-resilient-corridors). according to a sept. 28 announcement from u.s. rep. ayanna pressley and mayor michelle wu, the city argues that dot cited the project's electric-vehicle charging infrastructure as the reason for canceling the entire award. the announcement says that charging work represented less than 1% of project costs and that federal transportation officials had previously encouraged the city to include it. those are the city's allegations about the cancellation; the lawsuit has not produced a merits ruling (https://pressley.house.gov/2026/09/28/pressley-wu-announce-lawsuit-against-trump-administration-to-protect-20-million-federal-grant-for-roxburys-street-improvements/). the guardian independently reported that the case names transportation secretary sean duffy and was filed against the department over its decision to withdraw the money. the newspaper also reported the city's position that federal agencies cannot rewrite a program established by congress to match changing political priorities. the department's response was not included in the sources reviewed for this report, so the federal government's legal defense and any timetable for responding remain unclear (https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/28/boston-sues-trump-administration). the stakes are practical for people who use roxbury's busiest routes. boston says the project is meant to improve bus service, walking, bicycling and driving conditions at the same time. on its warren street project page, the city says more than 20,250 mbta riders use that corridor each weekday and that delays can add as much as 20 minutes to an average rider's day. that page predates the lawsuit and describes the broader transit problem rather than measuring the effect of the canceled grant, but it helps explain why the city treats the award as more than a budget line (https://content.boston.gov/departments/transportation/project/warren-street-bus-priority-corridor). roxbury's transportation history also shapes the argument. boston says the wide, vehicle-oriented corridors were created through eminent-domain and block-clearance decisions during the urban-renewal era of the 1960s. the city's current plan calls for safer crossings, more comfortable bus stops, shade and cooling spaces, bike infrastructure and green stormwater measures, while also trying to prevent displacement and support small businesses. those goals remain proposed project features, not completed improvements. the case arrives after the city had already approved accepting the federal award. a boston city council record from april 2025 describes the $20 million raise grant as funding to reconstruct and upgrade the three roxbury corridors. the city now says the cancellation removed a major share of the money needed to move the work forward. whether the court restores the award, sends the decision back to dot for reconsideration or leaves the cancellation in place will determine what boston can realistically build and when (https://content.boston.gov/departments/city-council/city-council-roll-call-votes?page=39). for now, the lawsuit is an opening filing, not a ruling that boston has won or that dot acted unlawfully. the public docket shows the case was assigned to u.s. district judge richard g. stearns after an initial judge recused himself on the filing date. the next meaningful developments will be the federal defendants' response, any request for interim relief and the court's decision on how the administrative procedure act claims proceed. until then, the three-corridor project remains listed by boston as pending, with its completion year undetermined. massachusetts massachusetts massachusetts ma boston roxbury, boston massachusetts boston roxbury transportation federal grants public transit crash that closed southbound i-91 in windsor thursday evening. one person was seriously injured thursday evening after being thrown from a vehicle in a two-car crash on interstate 91 south in windsor, connecticut state police said. the collision closed a section of the highway during the evening commute and remained under investigation overnight. connecticut department of transportation officials did not say whether speed, impairment, weather, a medical event or another factor played a role. those possibilities remain unconfirmed and should not be treated as explanations. the transportation ct-kosta-diamantis-sentenced-2026-09-30.excerpt: Kosta Diamantis was sentenced in absentia for extortion, bribery and false-statement convictions tied to school-construction contracts; federal authorities are still seeking him.
ct-kosta-diamantis-sentenced-2026-09-30.text: former connecticut official sentenced to 7 years after fleeing to greece kosta diamantis was sentenced in absentia for extortion, bribery and false-statement convictions tied to school-construction contracts; federal authorities are still seeking him. former connecticut school-construction official konstantinos “kosta” diamantis was sentenced wednesday to 84 months in federal prison and three years of supervised release, but he was not in the bridgeport courtroom to hear the punishment. the 70-year-old former state official had fled to greece before sentencing, and the u.s. attorney’s office for the district of connecticut said law enforcement is seeking him. the federal announcement is at https://www.justice.gov/usao-ct/pr/former-state-official-sentenced-7-years-federal-prison-school-construction-extortion-and. u.s. district judge stefan r. underhill imposed the sentence for convictions involving extortion, bribery, conspiracy and false statements. a federal jury in bridgeport found diamantis guilty in october 2025 on 21 counts: two counts of extortion, two extortion-conspiracy counts, two bribery counts, two bribery-conspiracy counts and 13 counts of making false statements to federal agents, according to the justice department. connecticut public reported that the case grew out of diamantis’s work as the state’s former deputy budget director and director of the office of school construction grants and review. that office administered grants for connecticut public-school construction projects seeking state funding. prosecutors said diamantis used the position to demand and receive payments from contractors while helping them obtain or preserve work. the justice department identified projects involving a school project in tolland, state reimbursement work for new britain and renovations at hartford’s bulkeley high school. the release says one contractor paid diamantis with cash and checks and hired his daughter at an inflated salary; those details describe the conduct underlying the convictions, not new untested allegations. the sentence came after an unusual break in the normal criminal-justice process. diamantis had been scheduled to appear for sentencing in september but did not attend. ct mirror reported that his lawyer told the court diamantis had left the united states and was in greece, where he holds dual citizenship. the later sentencing could proceed without him, but his absence leaves the practical question of how and when he will be taken into custody. federal officials have not announced that he has returned to the united states. the financial consequences are not settled. the justice department said judge underhill will determine restitution after additional court proceedings. that decision could identify losses that the government says were caused by the scheme, but the sentencing announcement did not give a final restitution amount. the unresolved figure matters because the projects at issue involved public school construction and state reimbursement, placing the case's consequences beyond the contractors and former official who appeared in court. the prison term was also shorter than the range sought by prosecutors. ct mirror reported that the government recommended a guideline range of 121 to 151 months, while the judge imposed 84 months. the difference does not change the convictions or the three-year supervised-release term, but it will be part of the record as prosecutors pursue diamantis and the court addresses restitution. ct mirror’s sentencing report is at https://ctmirror.org/2026/09/30/kosta-diamantis-still-a-fugitive-sentenced-to-84-months/. the case is not finished for the other people involved in the investigation. the justice department said contractors identified as duffy, monarca and roy pleaded guilty to related charges and are awaiting sentencing. the investigation was conducted by the fbi and irs criminal investigation, and federal prosecutors said the bribery scheme involved multimillion-dollar school-construction projects. connecticut public’s account of the sentencing, including the fact that diamantis remained outside the country, is at https://www.ctpublic.org/news/2026-09-30/kosta-diamantis-cts-disgraced-former-deputy-budget-director-sentenced. for connecticut, the public-interest question now extends from the sentence to the systems that allowed a senior official overseeing school-building money to steer contractors while concealing conduct from investigators. the court has established criminal responsibility through the jury’s verdict and the sentence; it has not yet completed restitution proceedings or resolved diamantis’s custody. those next steps will determine how much money is recovered, whether the former official is returned to face the prison term and what accountability reaches the related contractors. new-england new-england new england ct bridgeport bridgeport, ct-leap-attendance-grants-2026-09-30.excerpt: The new grants expand a home-visiting program that state officials say helped drive four straight years of lower chronic absenteeism, but the latest awards will still have to translate into local services.
ct-leap-attendance-grants-2026-09-30.text: connecticut awards $6.2m to 29 districts to improve student attendance the new grants expand a home-visiting program that state officials say helped drive four straight years of lower chronic absenteeism, but the latest awards will still have to translate into local services. connecticut is awarding approximately $6.2 million to 29 school districts and regional education organizations for a home-visiting program aimed at bringing chronically absent students back into regular contact with their schools. the grants, announced sept. 30 by gov. ned lamont and education commissioner charlene russell-tucker, are being distributed through the learner engagement and attendance program, known as leap. the money comes from a $7 million state budget line item. about $800,000 will support statewide infrastructure such as home-visitor training, program implementation and data collection, according to the [connecticut governor’s announcement](https://portal.ct.gov/governor/news/press-releases/2026/09-2026/governor-lamont-and-commissioner-russell-tucker-announce-state-grants-to-expand-program). leap pairs trained school staff and community partners with students and families. the visits are intended to identify the practical or personal barriers behind missed school days and connect families with services that can make regular attendance possible. the program began in 2021 with federal pandemic-relief money, initially serving 15 districts. it later expanded to 25, and this round brings the state’s reach to 29 districts for the 2026-27 school year. the recipients include some of connecticut’s largest districts. waterbury is slated to receive $525,000, hartford $500,000, bridgeport $475,000 and new haven $425,000. stamford will receive $350,000, while smaller awards go to districts including east windsor, east haven, plainfield and jamestown. middletown’s $125,000 award was reported separately by [middletown patch](https://patch.com/connecticut/middletown-ct/middletown-school-system-getting-6-figure-grant-aimed-boosting-attendance), which described the grant as funding for the same statewide leap effort. state officials say connecticut’s chronic-absenteeism rate fell from 23.7% in the 2021-22 school year to 16.4% in 2025-26. the governor’s office calculated that change as nearly 35,000 more students attending school regularly than at the earlier point. the figures describe statewide movement and do not establish that leap alone caused the decline; the announcement calls the program one part of a broader attendance strategy. there is earlier research behind the state’s decision to continue the program. the center for connecticut education research collaboration, a partnership involving the state education department and connecticut colleges, studied leap’s first 15 districts. its [published evaluation](https://portal.ct.gov/ccerc/current-projects/leap) found attendance gains after home visits, including an average increase of nearly 15 percentage points six months after visits for students served during the 2021-22 school year. the study also reported different effects by grade level and district, which matters because the new grant round includes a broader mix of communities than the initial cohort. connecticut says home visitors have conducted about 88,000 visits and reached roughly 53,000 students since leap began. those totals are cumulative program figures supplied by the state, not an independent count released with the new awards. the current announcement also does not provide a district-by-district attendance target or a deadline for demonstrating results. the immediate test will be local execution. districts will need to recruit or assign visitors, train them, coordinate with community organizations and turn conversations with families into help with transportation, health, housing, counseling or other barriers when those needs are identified. if the grants produce lasting attendance gains, connecticut will have a stronger case for making the home-visiting model a durable part of school operations after the pandemic-era funding that launched it has faded. new-england new-england new england ct hartford connecticut connecticut student attendance chronic absenteeism leap public schools education funding

ct-recreational-trails-grants-2026-10-01.excerpt: The grants will support construction, accessibility work, planning and maintenance, with half of the selected projects serving distressed municipalities or environmental-justice communities.
ct-recreational-trails-grants-2026-10-01.text: connecticut awards $10.5m for 50 recreational-trail projects the grants will support construction, accessibility work, planning and maintenance, with half of the selected projects serving distressed municipalities or environmental-justice communities. connecticut is awarding approximately $10.5 million to 50 projects intended to build, repair, connect and improve recreational trails across the state, gov. ned lamont and the department of energy and environmental protection announced thursday. the awards come through the connecticut recreational trails grant program after a competitive review by deep and the connecticut greenways council. the money was previously allocated by the state bond commission, according to the [governor’s announcement](https://portal.ct.gov/governor/news/press-releases/2026/10-2026/governor-lamont-announces-state-grants-for-recreational-trails). the program supports more than new stretches of pavement: the 2026 list includes construction, rehabilitation, bridge replacement, accessibility upgrades, trailhead and parking improvements, planning and design, equipment, outreach and long-term maintenance. that mix means the award will produce different kinds of results in different communities. winchester received $749,000 for construction intended to complete the sue grossman still river greenway. new haven received $274,730 for planning and design at the east rock park college woods inclusive community trail, while naugatuck received $400,000 to design a connector for the naugatuck river greenway between naugatuck and waterbury. bridgeport received $180,000 for planning and design of the old mill green pathways project, and east hartford received $200,000 to design a gap closure on the east coast greenway. the geographic spread is one reason the grants matter beyond individual trailheads. other awards include $505,000 for a multi-use connector in avon, $495,000 for an accessible bridge and trail at steep rock association’s hidden valley preserve, $492,874 for the university of connecticut’s trails and active-living program, and $498,400 for the connecticut forest and park association’s blue-blazed trail system and woodland conservation corps. the full award table also includes projects in eastern connecticut, the shoreline, the hartford region and the northwest hills. twenty-five of the 50 projects are in, or serve, municipalities the state classifies as distressed or environmental-justice communities. that designation does not mean every project has the same scope or construction schedule, but it signals that the review process gave weight to communities that have not always had equal access to outdoor recreation. the state says the awards are designed to improve public access while supporting recreation, active transportation, conservation and local connections. there is already evidence of substantial demand for the network. connecticut’s trail census, a uconn program that uses infrared counters and volunteer-supported data collection, recorded more than 2.7 million trail uses at 27 monitored locations during 2025, the state release said. the [uconn ct trails program](https://cttrails.uconn.edu/) maintains the census and a public trail-finder system; its 2025 count report is listed in the program’s [research archive](https://cttrails.uconn.edu/pubs/reports/). counter totals measure recorded uses at monitored sites, not every trip on every trail, so they should be read as an indicator rather than a statewide attendance total. the program also arrives as connecticut continues to treat trails as public-health and economic infrastructure. deep describes more than 2,000 miles of multi-use trails in state parks and forests alone, while the governor’s office said outdoor recreation contributes about $6 billion annually to the state economy and supports more than 50,000 jobs. those figures come from state and federal economic accounts cited in the announcement, not from an independent assessment of this grant round. the next phase will be local implementation. planning awards still require design work, permits and decisions about routes, access and maintenance before construction can begin. construction awards will need to be matched with contracting, scheduling and long-term upkeep. for residents, the practical question is when each town or organization can turn its award into a safer crossing, a more accessible trail, a completed connection or a maintained public route. the grant list provides the funding commitments; project timelines will depend on the recipients and the state’s agreement process. new-england new-england new england ct hartford connecticut connecticut ct-suffield-school-bus-crash-2026-10-01.text: suffield school bus crash sends 11 to hospitals with minor injuries a region 12 bus carrying students left south grand street and struck a building thursday morning; police said the cause remains under investigation. eleven people were taken to two local hospitals with minor injuries thursday after a small school bus carrying students left the roadway and struck a building in suffield, connecticut. the crash brought police, fire and ambulance crews to south grand street and left investigators working to determine why the bus veered off the road. suffield police said officers responded to the area of 425 south grand st. at about 9:49 a.m. after receiving a report of a motor-vehicle crash with possible injuries. their preliminary account said the bus was traveling north toward mountain road when it left the right shoulder and collided with a building beside the street. police did not announce a mechanical problem, medical event, weather factor or other cause. the bus came from regional school district 12, which serves communities in the shepaug valley. nbc connecticut reported that students were aboard, while the suffield volunteer ambulance association said 15 people, including the driver, were on the small bus. the association said 10 students and the driver were transported for evaluation. authorities did not release the students’ ages or identify the hospitals. the ambulance response required help from several nearby agencies. the ambulance association said it sent three ambulances staffed by paramedics, while enfield ems and the windsor locks lions club ambulance provided additional units. north central cmed helped coordinate the transports and contacted receiving hospitals to confirm that they could accommodate the patients. that coordination also shaped how the students were handled after the crash. according to the ambulance association’s statement reported by patch, responders tried to keep the students together when possible so school staff and families could receive information more easily. region 12 personnel came to the scene to assist the students, and emergency officials said the response was managed through the area’s normal mutual-aid system. the ambulance association also pushed back on online descriptions of the incident as a mass-casualty or multi-casualty event. it said the scene required significant coordination but did not meet that designation. that distinction describes the emergency-management classification, not the seriousness of the reported injuries: police and ambulance officials said everyone taken for treatment had minor injuries. hearst connecticut media reported that the bus was carrying shepaug valley school students on the way to a fair and that a region 12 official said the vehicle was driven by a properly licensed teacher. that account adds context to the trip but does not resolve the central unanswered question of what caused the bus to leave south grand street. police interviewed people involved and said the investigation was continuing. south grand street was closed while the scene was investigated and later reopened, according to local reports. no charges or citations had been announced in the available accounts. for families and residents, the immediate outcome was that the 11 people transported for care had reported minor injuries; the longer-term questions concern the crash sequence, the condition of the building and any findings by police or the school district. sources: [suffield police department details reported by patch](https://patch.com/connecticut/suffield/crash-reported-south-grand-street-suffield), [nbc connecticut](https://www.nbcconnecticut.com/news/local/11-people-sent-to-hospitals-after-school-bus-crashes-into-building-in-suffield/3780574/), ma-college-closure-risk-notice-2026-10-0.excerpt: Higher-education officials are planning an earlier public-warning deadline for financially distressed private colleges after two Massachusetts schools announced plans to close last spring.
ma-college-closure-risk-notice-2026-10-0.text: massachusetts colleges may have to disclose closure risk by dec. 31 higher-education officials are planning an earlier public-warning deadline for financially distressed private colleges after two massachusetts schools announced plans to close last spring. massachusetts higher-education officials are planning to require private colleges and universities judged to be at risk of imminent closure to post a public notice by dec. 31, an effort to give students, employees and surrounding communities more time to respond to a financial crisis. the proposed timing was described by outgoing department of higher education commissioner noe ortega during the board of higher education's sept. 29 meeting, according to wbur and the state house news service (https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/09/30/massachusetts-private-colleges-higher-ed-closing-risk-schools). the change would not mean that every school posting a notice is certain to shut down. under the state's financial assessment and risk monitoring, or farm, system, an institution is considered at risk of imminent closure when the commissioner determines that it may be unable to continue operations or substantially meet its obligations to enrolled and admitted students through the current and following academic year. the massachusetts department of higher education says the system is intended to identify risks, monitor mitigation plans and reduce disruption to students, families, faculty, staff and host communities (https://www.mass.edu/strategic/farm.asp). the state already requires colleges to alert the board of higher education about known financial liabilities or risks that could lead to an imminent closure or prevent the institution from fulfilling its obligations. the department's farm materials say those immediate notifications are confidential, while public notice is part of a later process if the institution's financial condition remains sufficiently uncertain after review and risk-mitigation planning. the department also requires private institutions to post annual financial reports and plain-language summaries on their websites. the proposed dec. 31 date is meant to make the public-warning process more predictable. wbur reported that current regulations use dec. 1 as the annual threshold measurement date for deciding whether a college can meet its obligations for the rest of the current academic year and the next one, while the board currently has flexibility about when after that date to make a determination. board chairman chris gabrieli said a december determination would reduce the risk that students and staff learn about a potential closure only after they have made plans for the spring semester. the discussion follows two massachusetts closures announced near the end of the last academic year. anna maria college in paxton and hampshire college in amherst cited financial difficulties in announcing plans to close, wbur reported. hampshire's public notice from the department of higher education says the college planned to end academic programming at the end of 2026 while continuing academic programs, residential support and transition services for enrolled students through dec. 31 (https://www.mass.edu/strategic/documents/2026-04-14-hampshire-noitce-posting-for-dhe-website.pdf). the notice also says the department could not confirm that hampshire had enough resources to sustain current operations and fulfill obligations through the current and subsequent academic years; that is a regulatory finding, not a claim that every massachusetts college faces the same condition. massachusetts has been building this oversight system since the sudden 2018 closure of mount ida college. the department says 24 colleges and universities closed, merged or began winding down between 2014 and 2022, and that the 2019 farm law and later regulations were designed to improve financial monitoring and closure planning. those rules can require a contingency plan covering student deposits and records, and in some cases a bond or letter of credit to help protect those obligations. the department's current process describes screening from november through april, review of risk-mitigation plans from june through october, and determinations and contingency planning in november and december. officials also said the board plans to add staff and use outside firms to strengthen financial assessments, while revising required training for private-college trustees. the goal, gabrieli said, is to give students time to identify transfer options, give faculty and staff a reasonable period to seek other work, and reduce the shock to communities that depend on a campus. the timing matters this fall because ortega's term as commissioner ended sept. 30 and josé luis santos began serving as interim commissioner on oct. 1, according to the department (https://www.mass.edu/). the public-warning deadline remains a planned policy change rather than a newly announced closure list. the next questions are whether the board of higher education formally adopts the dec. 31 timetable, which institutions are identified through the annual farm review, and what mitigation or teach-out plans follow. until those steps occur, students should not read the proposed deadline as evidence that a particular college is about to close; it is an attempt to move information earlier when the state does determine that a school's finances may threaten its ability to serve students. massachusetts massachusetts ma-cranberry-harvest-quality-2026-10-02.excerpt: The state is celebrating October as Cranberry Month while UMass Amherst’s final 2026 forecast warns of very poor keeping quality for the crop, adding a food-supply and farm-management challenge to the seasonal harvest.
ma-cranberry-harvest-quality-2026-10-02.text: massachusetts cranberry harvest opens with industry facing poor keeping-quality forecast the state is celebrating october as cranberry month while umass amherst’s final 2026 forecast warns of very poor keeping quality for the crop, adding a food-supply and farm-management challenge to the seasonal harvest. massachusetts is beginning its annual cranberry harvest under two competing headlines: state officials are promoting october as cranberry month, while the university of massachusetts amherst’s cranberry station says the 2026 crop has a very poor keeping-quality forecast. the warning does not by itself predict the size of the harvest or say that every bog will be affected in the same way. it does mean growers and buyers are entering the season with a documented concern about how well harvested fruit will hold after it leaves the bog. gov. maura healey proclaimed october as massachusetts cranberry month on oct. 1 at makepeace farms in wareham, where the massachusetts department of agricultural resources gathered with growers and local officials to mark the start of the harvest. the department says massachusetts has about 11,500 acres of commercial cranberry bogs, concentrated in southeastern massachusetts, cape cod and the islands. its announcement is available at https://www.mass.gov/news/governor-healey-proclaims-october-as-massachusetts-cranberry-month. the state describes cranberries as massachusetts’ leading agricultural food commodity crop. the department estimates the industry supports more than 6,400 jobs and generates more than $1.7 billion in economic impact. those are statewide economic estimates supplied by the administration, not a measure of this year’s harvest revenue. the same announcement says cranberry growers help protect more than 60,000 acres of undeveloped open space, making the industry relevant to land use and conservation as well as food production. the quality warning comes from umass amherst’s cranberry station, the university extension and research program serving the state’s growers. its june 12 final 2026 keeping quality forecast describes the massachusetts crop’s keeping quality as “very poor.” the station lists that forecast at https://www.umass.edu/agriculture-food-environment/cranberry/news. keeping quality is different from total acreage, yield or price: a forecast about storage performance does not establish how many berries will be harvested or what consumers will pay for them. that program. those projects, according to the department, have modernized 533 acres and supported irrigation, water management, specialized equipment and automation. the stated goals are to improve as ways to remove nitrogen before it reaches cape cod waters. that project is not a measure of the commercial harvest, but it shows why bogs matter beyond the crop: working farms, retired agricultural land, groundwater and coastal ecosystems are connected in southeastern massachusetts. the gbh report is at https://www.wgbh.org/news/local/2026-10-01/gbh-daily-into-the-bog. october’s proclamation ma-life-sciences-tax-incentives-2026-09-.excerpt: The awards span 38 companies, with most of the expected new positions located outside Boston and Cambridge and commitments subject to three years of reporting.
ma-life-sciences-tax-incentives-2026-09-.text: massachusetts awards nearly $40m in life-science tax incentives tied to 1,644 jobs the awards span 38 companies, with most of the expected new positions located outside boston and cambridge and commitments subject to three years of reporting. massachusetts has awarded nearly $40 million in tax incentives to 38 life-science companies that collectively pledged to create 1,644 new jobs, putting a statewide economic-development program behind expansions in research, therapeutics, diagnostics and manufacturing. gov. maura healey announced the awards sept. 28 at smc ltd. in devens. the figures describe company commitments, not jobs already filled or money paid directly to workers. (https://www.mass.gov/news/governor-healey-announces-40-million-to-grow-massachusetts-life-sciences-industry-create-more-than-1600-jobs) the geographic distribution is a central feature of this round. the massachusetts life sciences center said 31 of the 38 awardees are expanding outside boston and cambridge, and those projects account for 71% of the expected new jobs. that puts communities such as acton, andover, bedford, burlington, chelmsford, devens, framingham, marlborough, milford, northbridge, sudbury, waltham and woburn in the direct path of the announced hiring commitments, rather than limiting the benefit to the state's traditional laboratory hubs. the agency described the program as a way to use massachusetts' broader network of life-science assets for growth and retention. (https://www.mass.gov/news/governor-healey-announces-40-million-to-grow-massachusetts-life-sciences-industry-create-more-than-1600-jobs) the largest individual award goes to acton-based insulet corporation: $10 million tied to a 250-job commitment. lila sciences in cambridge received $3.6 million for 200 jobs, while vertex pharmaceuticals in boston received $3.025 million for 121 jobs. other sizable awards include $2.875 million for bristol myers squibb's 125-job commitment in devens, $1.86 million for transmedics in andover, and $1.35 million for smc's 54 jobs in devens. the boston business journal reported that the full list also includes astrazeneca, vericel, zoll medical, rentschler biopharma and dozens of smaller firms. (https://www.bizjournals.com/boston/news/2026/09/28/mass-tax-incentive-program-2026.html) the awards are tax incentives administered through the massachusetts life sciences center's tax incentive program jointly with the department of revenue. the program is open to companies doing research and development, commercialization or manufacturing in massachusetts, and the commitments are meant to be new, long-term positions. awardees must maintain their job commitments for three years and file regular reports documenting the jobs created as a result of the incentives. that structure makes the announced 1,644 jobs a measurable target that can be checked over time, rather than an immediate headcount. the state release also says the program has supported commitments for more than 22,300 jobs since the center was established. (https://www.mass.gov/news/governor-healey-announces-40-million-to-grow-massachusetts-life-sciences-industry-create-more-than-1600-jobs) demand for the program was stronger than the award total. the boston business journal reported that companies submitted $58 million in applications this year, compared with a previous year when the center needed two rounds to allocate the full $40 million authorization. the outlet also reported that, since 2009, the center has made 519 awards to nearly 300 distinct companies totaling about $422 million and tied to more than 22,300 jobs. those figures show both the scale of the state's strategy and the competitive choices behind this year's list: the program is not an open-ended subsidy for every applicant, and some proposals were not funded in this cycle. (https://www.bizjournals.com/boston/news/2026/09/28/mass-tax-incentive-program-2026.html) the current ceiling comes from the 2024 mass leads act, which raised the annual statutory cap for life-science tax incentives from $30 million to $40 million and broadened the eligible field to include areas such as medical technology, preventative medicine, biosecurity and life-science-related artificial intelligence. massachusetts' technical tax guidance describes the program as a collection of tax incentives available to qualifying companies, rather than a single grant pot. that distinction matters when evaluating the public return: the state is trading foregone tax revenue for promised hiring and investment, while the companies still have to execute their expansion plans. (https://www.mass.gov/technical-information-release/tir-25-5-tax-provisions-in-certain-massachusetts-legislation-enacted-in-2024) for workers and municipalities, the next test is delivery. companies must meet the hiring and retention conditions attached to their awards, and the state must report whether projects translate into sustained employment across the commonwealth. the announcement includes activity in artificial intelligence, women's health, therapeutics, diagnostics, medical technology, research and development and biomanufacturing. if the commitments hold, the round will distribute new positions across a wider geography and reinforce massachusetts' life-science supply chain; if projects fall short, the reporting and tax-administration process will determine how the state responds. the award announcement establishes the targets, but future compliance records will show how many jobs actually materialize. massachusetts massachusetts massachusetts ma massachusetts massachusetts life sciences tax incentives jobs economic development biotechnology

ma-masshealth-immigrant-coverage-2026-10.excerpt: A federal eligibility change taking effect Oct. 1 moves some lawfully present immigrants from full MassHealth coverage to narrower programs, while others remain eligible for comprehensive care.
ma-masshealth-immigrant-coverage-2026-10.text: masshealth coverage changes reach 7,300 immigrants in massachusetts a federal eligibility change taking effect oct. 1 moves some lawfully present immigrants from full masshealth coverage to narrower programs, while others remain eligible for comprehensive care. a federal eligibility change took effect thursday for about 7,300 massachusetts residents who are lawfully present immigrants and receive masshealth, the state’s medicaid program. the change does not apply to u.s. citizens or nationals, and it does not end coverage for every immigrant in the affected legal categories. it changes which federal and state-funded coverage programs are available to particular members based on immigration status, age, pregnancy, disability and other eligibility factors, according to the [masshealth information page](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/masshealth-information-for-noncitizens) and a september eligibility memo to state staff. the affected groups can include refugees, people granted asylum, some humanitarian parolees, certain survivors of abuse or trafficking and other categories that federal law previously treated as eligible for comprehensive medicaid. masshealth estimates that approximately 7,300 members are affected in massachusetts. the [boston globe reported](https://www.bostonglobe.com/2026/09/29/metro/masshealth-medicaid-immigrants-refugees/) that more than 8,000 additional people in connecticut, maine, new hampshire, rhode island and vermont are expected to lose comprehensive coverage in the same federal change, putting the massachusetts shift inside a wider new england disruption. the practical result will not be identical for everyone. children younger than 21 and people who are pregnant or postpartum generally keep their prior comprehensive coverage under the state’s guidance. older adults and disabled adults who meet income and asset rules can generally move to masshealth family assistance, which continues to provide comprehensive coverage but has different program rules. some other adults will move to masshealth limited and the health safety net, programs that can help pay for emergency services or medically necessary care at participating hospitals and community health centers but do not replace the full range of masshealth standard benefits. the [gbh report](https://www.wgbh.org/news/local/2026-09-21/health-advocates-warn-of-masshealth-changes-for-immigrants-coming-oct-1) described the change as a loss of full standard or care plus coverage for certain immigrants. health advocates told gbh that some members will be moved to family assistance while others will have only masshealth limited and health safety net coverage. the distinction matters at the point of care: a narrower program may help with an emergency or a qualifying visit without covering routine primary care, most prescriptions, dental care, vision care or long-term services in the same way as comprehensive coverage. masshealth and community organizations have been notifying members in stages. health care for all told gbh that notices went to roughly 2,000 people in june and more than 5,000 in july and august, followed by final notices explaining the member’s new status and appeal rights. the state’s public guidance says affected members should review their notices, respond to requests for information and use the state’s screening and assistance resources rather than assume that an immigration-status change affects everyone in the same way. the change is likely to be felt most heavily in the state’s immigrant-serving health and social-service networks. health care for all identified suffolk, middlesex, essex and worcester counties as having the largest shares of affected immigrants covered through connectorcare, with spanish, brazilian portuguese, haitian creole, chinese and russian among the languages spoken by people receiving outreach. those county and language figures describe where advocates expect communication needs, not a count of every affected masshealth member. the immediate coverage change also arrives before a second phase of federal medicaid changes. masshealth says some adults ages 19 through 64 will face new work or education reporting requirements and more frequent renewals beginning in january 2027. massachusetts has launched a statewide campaign with health care for all and community organizations to help members understand those rules, but the state must implement the federal requirements while trying to limit avoidable coverage losses. for massachusetts residents, the next step is individual rather than political: check the notice from masshealth, confirm which program is listed, and ask for help if the decision appears to overlook age, pregnancy, disability, income or immigration documents. the state’s published rules make clear that being lawfully present is not itself a guarantee of one particular masshealth category, but neither does the oct. 1 change mean that all immigrants lose health coverage. the outcome depends on the member’s full eligibility record and on whether the person uses the appeal process when the state’s determination is disputed. massachusetts massachusetts massachusetts ma boston massachusetts massachusetts masshealth medicaid ma-one-stop-growth-awards-2026-10-02.excerpt: The largest Community One Stop for Growth round to date is expected to support more than 27,000 homes and 13,000 permanent jobs, with South Coast communities receiving $6.5 million for housing, infrastructure and downtown reuse.
ma-one-stop-growth-awards-2026-10-02.text: massachusetts awards $330m for housing and local growth projects the largest community one stop for growth round to date is expected to support more than 27,000 homes and 13,000 permanent jobs, with south coast communities receiving $6.5 million for housing, infrastructure and downtown reuse. massachusetts is directing $330 million to 403 housing and economic-development projects in 207 communities, the healey administration announced oct. 1. state officials say the fiscal 2027 community one stop for growth awards are the largest single round in the program's history and are expected to support more than 27,000 new homes, more than 13,000 permanent jobs and more than 7 million square feet of commercial development. the administration also estimates that the projects could help unlock $24.6 billion in private investment. those are projected results, not homes or jobs already delivered. the awards are designed to help cities, towns and other organizations move projects from planning to construction or reuse. the state describes the community one stop for growth as a coordinated application and review process for housing and economic-development programs, rather than a single construction grant. the current awards are being administered through 14 programs involving the executive office of economic development, the executive office of housing and livable communities, and massdevelopment, according to the massachusetts municipal association's account of the announcement. the state's program overview is available at https://www.mass.gov/info-details/community-one-stop-for-growth. the largest portions of the round are aimed at infrastructure that can make development possible. the massachusetts municipal association reported $109.7 million for 54 housingworks infrastructure projects, $105.1 million for 59 massworks projects and $51.1 million for 24 mbta community catalyst fund projects. other awards cover underused properties, seaport-related work, rural development, downtown improvements, site readiness, planning and brownfield redevelopment. the mix matters because a housing proposal can stall for reasons that are not solved by building financing alone, including streets, utilities, site cleanup and public-space improvements. the geographic reach is also part of the administration's case for the program. the awards extend to every region of massachusetts, and the municipal association said 13 communities are receiving one stop funding for the first time. the administration's breakdown, as reported by the association, puts 36% of projects in rural communities, 24% in gateway cities, 37% in housing choice communities and about half in mbta communities. that distribution describes the locations of awarded projects; it does not guarantee that each community will produce the number of homes or jobs projected for the statewide round. on the south coast, new bedford-area communities are set to receive $6.5 million, according to new bedford guide. new bedford's share totals $4,079,800, including $600,000 for repairs and life-safety upgrades at the star store in the downtown arts district. the work is intended to help artists and creative developers reoccupy the building as it moves toward a planned 2027 reopening. another $900,000 will support the conversion of a vacant former nursing home on acushnet avenue into dozens of workforce-housing units, while other awards address riverside development, waterfront and downtown lighting, and public-safety infrastructure. the local report is at https://www.newbedfordguide.com/6-5-million-awarded-economic-development-grants-new-bedford-senate-district/2026/10/01. dartmouth is slated to receive $2.265 million, most of it for sewer-pump improvements and replacements intended to add capacity for new housing, new bedford guide reported. a smaller dartmouth award will study potential uses for a former police station. fairhaven will use funding for improvements around the pease park boating area, including stormwater work and public amenities, while mattapoisett will develop standards for its village business district. those local examples show how the statewide program combines housing production with the less visible infrastructure and planning work that supports it. the massachusetts municipal association, which represents the state's cities and towns, said local governments often lack the resources to take on projects of this scale without state partnerships. that is an advocacy group's assessment, not an independent evaluation of the awards' economic return. for residents, the practical test will be whether the money leads to completed infrastructure, occupied homes, reopened commercial space and sustained employment rather than remaining at the announcement stage. the state says the full list of recipients and project descriptions is available through its community one stop for growth awards dashboard at https://www.mass.gov/info-details/community-one-stop-for-growth-awards. the program schedule says contracting is expected to begin in november 2026. project timing will vary by municipality and grant program, so the next milestones are contracting, local approvals and construction or reuse work. the oct. 1 announcement establishes the awards and their projected benefits; later records will show which projects advance and which targets are ultimately met. massachusetts massachusetts massachusetts ma boston massachusetts massachusetts housing ma-project-rare-gas-pipeline-review-2026.excerpt: Project RARE would replace and add sections of Enbridge's Algonquin system in Massachusetts and Rhode Island, a proposal supporters tie to winter energy costs and critics say would prolong fossil-fuel dependence.
ma-project-rare-gas-pipeline-review-2026.text: healey urges faster federal review of new england gas pipeline expansion project rare would replace and add sections of enbridge's algonquin system in massachusetts and rhode island, a proposal supporters tie to winter energy costs and critics say would prolong fossil-fuel dependence. massachusetts gov. maura healey is asking the federal government to move faster on its review of a proposed natural-gas pipeline expansion that would reach into massachusetts and rhode island. in a letter to u.s. energy secretary chris wright, healey said the reliable affordable resilient enhancement project, known as project rare, could lower costs for about 600,000 customers. her request does not approve the project: federal regulators are still in the pre-filing environmental-review stage. the governor's letter is the latest turn in a regional argument over how to handle new england's high winter energy costs. healey's administration says constrained gas supply on the coldest days can push power plants toward more expensive oil and force utilities to buy liquefied natural gas. the administration is asking for a timely review while saying environmental review and community engagement should continue. the massachusetts announcement is at https://www.mass.gov/news/governor-healey-calls-on-trump-administration-to-expedite-review-of-gas-pipeline-expansion. project rare is being developed by enbridge along its algonquin natural-gas system, which runs from new jersey through new york and southern new england. wbur reported that the proposal would replace about eight miles of existing pipe with larger-diameter pipe in massachusetts and rhode island, add a parallel section in rhode island and upgrade a compressor station in cromwell, connecticut. enbridge has said the expansion would add roughly 75 million cubic feet per day of capacity. wbur's report is at https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/10/01/governor-healey-project-rare-natural-gas-pipeline-expansion-fossil-fuels-climate. federal records provide a more detailed picture of the footprint. the federal energy regulatory commission says the planned facilities total about 13.5 miles in massachusetts and rhode island. the proposal includes replacing about 8.25 miles of 16-inch pipe with 36-inch pipe in norfolk and worcester counties and providence county, rhode island; installing about 2.2 miles of 12-inch looping pipe in newport county; and adding three miles of 36-inch looping pipe in providence county. it also includes software-related compression changes at the cromwell station. ferc's project page, docket pf26-7-000, says the project has not been approved: https://www.ferc.gov/algonquin-gas-transmission-enhancement-project. the local stakes extend beyond a construction map. ferc says the project is intended to increase supply to local distribution companies and improve regional reliability, while the massachusetts administration and eversource have connected new capacity to lower winter reliance on liquefied natural gas. wbur reported that massachusetts regulators approved a 10-year eversource purchase plan tied to the expansion and that the state estimates it could reduce the utility's liquefied-natural-gas use by about $40 million annually. that estimate is a projected benefit, not a guaranteed reduction on a household bill. the project is also colliding with massachusetts' climate requirements and a broader fight over the role of gas in the regional grid. wbur reported that climate advocates questioned whether adding pipeline capacity could lock in more gas use even if it reduces short-term reliance on liquefied natural gas. conservation law foundation said healey's request repeated a claim about lower heating costs that the group disputes, arguing that cleaner hydroelectric and offshore-wind deliveries have been the more reliable source of price containment. clf's response is at https://www.clf.org/newsroom/clf-challenges-gas-pipeline-push/. ferc's pre-filing process is not the final permitting decision. the agency describes it as a pre-application phase designed to surface environmental issues before an official application, with opportunities for public comments, open houses and scoping sessions. that means residents, landowners and communities along the proposed work areas still have a formal role as the record develops. the agency's page lists earlier 2026 open houses in wrentham and bellingham, massachusetts, and in several rhode island communities; later filings and notices will determine the next steps. for massachusetts, the immediate question is whether faster federal attention produces a faster decision without narrowing the review. healey is positioning project rare as one response to costly winter energy constraints, while environmental groups warn that the long-term answer must reduce dependence on fossil fuels. until enbridge files the project for full federal review and regulators evaluate its environmental and reliability claims, the expansion remains a proposal rather than new pipeline capacity. the review, and the debate over who should bear its costs and risks, now moves forward on two tracks. massachusetts massachusetts massachusetts ma ma-public-benefit-fraud-auditor-report-2.excerpt: A new state report says investigators identified fraudulent overpayments in 402 cases from January through June, while agencies had finalized $285,339 in civil recoveries and restitution settlements.
ma-public-benefit-fraud-auditor-report-2.text: massachusetts auditor identifies $10.6m in public-benefit fraud, reports limited recoveries a new state report says investigators identified fraudulent overpayments in 402 cases from january through june, while agencies had finalized $285,339 in civil recoveries and restitution settlements. massachusetts state auditor diana dizoglio's office said wednesday that its bureau of special investigations identified $10.6 million in public-benefit fraud during the first six months of 2026, a finding that puts new numbers around losses in programs used for health care, food assistance and family support. the report covers january 1 through june 30 and is based on investigations completed by the bureau, not on criminal convictions in every case. (https://www.mass.gov/news/auditor-dizoglios-bureau-of-special-investigations-identifies-over-106-million-in-public-benefit-fraud) the bureau investigated 2,223 cases during the period and calculated overpayments in 402 cases where it identified fraud, according to the state auditor's report. masshealth and medicaid accounted for the largest share: $6,051,185, or 57% of the total. the supplemental nutrition assistance program accounted for another $3,854,119, or 36.3%. personal care attendant services represented $538,332, followed by $130,483 in transitional aid to families with dependent children and $38,463 in emergency aid to the elderly, disabled, and children. the categories add up to $10,612,582. the distribution matters because the reported losses touch programs with different administrators and different kinds of eligibility records. masshealth helps pay for medical care, snap helps eligible households buy food, and cash-assistance programs support families or people facing emergencies. a finding of an improper payment does not by itself establish who caused it or whether a criminal case will follow; the report describes the bureau's investigative findings and overpayment calculations, while other agencies handle enforcement and collection. the pace of identified fraud was higher than in the preceding six-month reporting period. boston 25 news, reviewing the new report, said the auditor's office had identified about $4.4 million in the prior period. the station also reported that the latest total included two dental providers accused of billing masshealth for “impossible days,” including days when their offices were closed. the report does not name suspected fraudsters, and the figures should be read as a snapshot of cases completed during the reporting period rather than a complete measure of all improper payments in massachusetts. (https://cmg-cmg-tv-10020-prod.cdn.arcpublishing.com/news/local/25-investigates-106m-benefits-fraud-little-clawed-back/tdd6wuwflre3xau536qiw6ac5a/) the state's recovery figures are much smaller than the amount identified. the report lists $285,339 in restitution settlements and civil recoveries for the two quarters combined, roughly 2.7% of the $10.6 million identified. that comparison does not mean the remaining amount is permanently unrecoverable: the auditor says restitution settlements continue beyond the report, and the programs that administer the benefits are responsible for collection activity. the lag does show why an investigation announcement and a completed recovery are different stages of public accountability. the quarterly split also shows where the total accumulated. in the third quarter of the state's fiscal year, the bureau investigated 994 cases and identified fraud in 168 cases, with overpayments totaling $2,981,696. in the fourth quarter, it investigated 1,229 cases and identified fraud in 234 cases, with overpayments totaling $7,630,886. the report says the fourth-quarter figures include the resumption of referrals through the document benefit fraud task force and two dental-provider cases involving alleged billing for impossible days. the bureau of special investigations operates within the office of the state auditor and can investigate allegations involving programs administered by the department of transitional assistance, the department of children and families and the division of medical assistance, which runs masshealth. its authority does not include collecting settlements or prosecuting cases. those decisions move to the relevant benefit programs and, when appropriate, state or federal prosecutors. boston 25 reported that the executive office of health and human services defended its program-integrity processes while saying agencies had referred most of the cases to the auditor's office. for residents, the report's immediate significance is less about a single statewide bill than about how quickly suspected overpayments are detected, referred and recovered. the auditor's office is asking people with information about possible public-assistance fraud to use its anonymous reporting channels, including the bureau of special investigations hotline at (617) 727-6771. the next measurable steps will be agency decisions on disqualification, civil recoupment or prosecution, along with any future reports showing how much of the identified money is ultimately recovered. massachusetts ma-snap-admin-cost-shift-2026-10-01.excerpt: A federal law cuts Washington's share of state SNAP operating costs from 50% to 25%, adding an estimated $53 million to Massachusetts' current-year burden as eligibility work and call-center demand remain under pressure.
ma-snap-admin-cost-shift-2026-10-01.text: massachusetts takes on larger snap administration bill as federal share drops a federal law cuts washington's share of state snap operating costs from 50% to 25%, adding an estimated $53 million to massachusetts' current-year burden as eligibility work and call-center demand remain under pressure. massachusetts is beginning a new federal fiscal year with a larger bill for running the supplemental nutrition assistance program, after a federal law reduced washington's share of state administrative costs from 50% to 25%. the change affects the machinery behind snap — including eligibility processing, benefit issuance and related systems — rather than directly removing the federal dollars loaded onto households' electronic benefit cards. wbur reported that the shift requires massachusetts to absorb an estimated additional $53 million during the current fiscal year. the change comes from section 10106 of public law 119-21, the reconciliation law enacted in july 2025. the u.s. government publishing office's text says the federal government will cover 50% of eligible state administrative costs through fiscal year 2026, then 25% beginning in fiscal year 2027. because the federal fiscal year began oct. 1, 2026, the lower reimbursement rate is now in effect. the law is available at https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/plaw-119publ21/html/plaw-119publ21.htm. the u.s. department of agriculture's food and nutrition administration described the same change in a june proposed rule. the agency said the rule would update snap regulations to match the law, while leaving the categories of allowable administrative expenses and the basic reimbursement procedures in place. the proposal is at https://www.fna.usda.gov/snap/fr-062426. that distinction matters: the statute has changed the funding split, while usda's rulemaking is the regulatory step explaining how the change fits into existing program rules. for massachusetts, the new expense arrives while the agency that administers snap is already under strain. wbur reported that federal data showed enrollment in the state had fallen by nearly 190,000 after the 2025 law added eligibility requirements. the report also said the department of transitional assistance faces a lawsuit alleging that roughly 80% of snap-related calls have been dropped. those are reported conditions and allegations, not a finding that every missed call or enrollment change was caused by the cost-sharing provision. the operating-cost change is separate from the annual adjustment to household benefits. massachusetts' department of transitional assistance says the maximum monthly allotment for one person rose from $291 to $292 effective oct. 1, while the maximum for a four-person household rose from $973 to $975. the agency cautions that most households do not receive the maximum; income, shelter, utility, child-care and certain medical deductions affect the individual calculation. its table is available at https://www.mass.gov/info-details/snap-cost-of-living-adjustments-cola. that separation helps explain why families may see a small benefit increase even as the state faces higher administrative costs. the federal government continues to finance the underlying snap allotments, but massachusetts must find more state money for the workers, technology and customer service needed to determine eligibility and deliver those benefits. food-assistance organizations told wbur the cost shift adds pressure at a time when the department is understaffed. the law also sets up a possible second financial exposure. starting in a later fiscal year, states can be required to share part of the cost of snap benefits based on payment-error rates. wbur cited a center on budget and policy priorities estimate that massachusetts could face as much as $350 million in additional costs under that provision, but that figure is an outside estimate rather than a current bill or a final federal assessment. the timing and amount would depend on the rules and the state's measured error rate. the immediate question for massachusetts is how the administration and legislature will cover the $53 million administrative gap without slowing applications, renewals or case assistance. people receiving snap can check their current balance and notices through dta connect or the phone number on the back of their ebt card, while advocates and food banks are watching whether the added state obligation shows up as longer waits or more demand for emergency groceries. the federal cost shift is settled; its effect on service quality will become clearer as the state operates under the new funding formula. massachusetts massachusetts ma-somerville-teele-square-fire-2026-10-.excerpt: A five-alarm blaze damaged 32 homes and a row of ground-floor businesses Wednesday; the city and Somerville Homeless Coalition have opened an emergency fund as the cause remains under investigation.
ma-somerville-teele-square-fire-2026-10-.text: teele square fire displaces 43 somerville residents and closes six businesses a five-alarm blaze damaged 32 homes and a row of ground-floor businesses wednesday; the city and somerville homeless coalition have opened an emergency fund as the cause remains under investigation. somerville officials and the somerville homeless coalition have activated an emergency fund for 43 residents displaced by a five-alarm fire that damaged a teele square building wednesday. the city of somerville said thursday that the blaze affected 32 homes at 1137-1147 broadway, and that every resident escaped safely. city staff and the american red cross were helping residents find temporary accommodations and meet immediate needs. the fire began around 4:50 p.m. september 30 and continued for more than three hours, according to the cambridge-somerville independent (https://csindie.com/more-than-40-people-are-displaced-after-teele-square-fire-chief-says/). the three-story brick building, also described in reports as 1135 broadway, suffered heavy fire, smoke and water damage on its third floor and roof. the lower floors sustained extensive water damage, maine-aclu-birthright-citizenship-lawsui.excerpt: ACLU affiliates in Maine, New Hampshire and Massachusetts joined a federal lawsuit challenging President Trump's August order, while an earlier injunction remains in place.
maine-aclu-birthright-citizenship-lawsui.text: new england groups file fresh challenge to birthright citizenship order aclu affiliates in maine, new hampshire and massachusetts joined a federal lawsuit challenging president trump's august order, while an earlier injunction remains in place. a new federal lawsuit led in part by the aclu of maine is asking a washington, d.c., court to block the trump administration's latest attempt to narrow birthright citizenship. the case, nathan v. trump, was filed sept. 28 in the u.s. district court for the district of columbia, according to the public docket. the coalition includes the national aclu, aclu affiliates in maine, new hampshire, massachusetts and the district of columbia, the legal defense fund, the asian law caucus and the democracy defenders fund. the groups say the order violates the constitution and federal citizenship law; those are allegations in a newly filed complaint, not a ruling by the court (https://dockets.justia.com/docket/district-of-columbia/dcdce/1:2026cv03377/297026). the lawsuit targets executive order 14418, which president donald trump signed aug. 6 and the federal register published aug. 11. the order directs federal agencies not to issue documents recognizing u.s. citizenship, or accept state and local documents purporting to recognize it, when neither parent is a u.s. citizen and specified conditions apply. those conditions include a parent classified as an alien enemy, certain foreign-government or international-organization employees, and a parent alleged to have used a commercial transaction or fraud to obtain citizenship. the order also addresses some births in u.s. territories where federal law does not confer citizenship (https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/eo-14418.pdf). the filing's practical reach is broader than the phrase “birth tourism” often used in public debate. the order specifically refers to arrangements in which a parent pays to ensure that a mother is in the united states to give birth or pays a surrogate who is in the country. it also gives agencies enforcement responsibilities, including the state department, justice department, department of homeland security and social security administration. if implemented, those instructions could affect how families obtain or use federal citizenship documentation, although the order's ultimate legal effect is now being contested in court. the plaintiffs' legal theory relies on the fourteenth amendment's citizenship clause and the federal statute that codifies birthright citizenship. the complaint cites the supreme court's 1898 decision in united states v. wong kim ark and says the constitution does not allow the president to create new exceptions by executive order. the filing also points to the supreme court's june decision in trump v. barbara, which the aclu says rejected the administration's earlier, broader order. the associated press separately reported that the supreme court struck down that earlier attempt before the administration issued the narrower august order (https://www.aclumaine.org/app/uploads/2026/09/nathan-v.-trump-complaint.pdf; https://apnews.com/article/trump-again-tries-to-restrict-birthright-citizenship-after-supreme-court-ruling-494add8239eb1c0c9f4ccb45db03f1f0). for new england, the case places legal organizations from three states in the next phase of the fight. aclu of maine legal director carol garvan is quoted in the group's announcement as arguing that the supreme court's decision prevents the president or congress from ending birthright citizenship. aclu affiliates are advocacy organizations, not state governments, so maine, new hampshire and massachusetts are not plaintiffs as states in this case. the https://www.mainepublic.org/immigration/2026-09-28/aclu-of-maine-sues-trump-administration-over-latest-attempt-to-restrict-birthright-citizenship). the public d.c. docket lists the sept. 28 complaint and motions asking the court to let the plaintiffs proceed under pseudonyms and file later exhibits under seal. it did not list a merits ruling as of the docket's sept. 28 retrieval date. the next important steps will be the government's response and any decision on a request for preliminary relief. until then, the complaint records the challengers' claims, the executive order records the
